title: Acute liver failure
subject: gastroenterology
setting: Emergency department, ICU, liver transplant centre
summary: INR 1.5 or more with any encephalopathy and no prior liver disease: contact a transplant centre early, give IV N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol and early-grade non-paracetamol ALF), move to ICU at grade 2 encephalopathy, protect against cerebral oedema (sodium 145 to 150 mmol/L, early CRRT for hyperammonaemia) and apply King's College criteria.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Definition: liver injury with coagulopathy (INR 1.5 or more) and any degree of encephalopathy, illness under 26 weeks, in a patient without pre-existing liver disease. Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis and Budd-Chiari syndrome can qualify despite underlying disease.
Distinguish from decompensated cirrhosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure, which are managed differently.

Hyperacute presentations (paracetamol, hepatitis A and E, ischaemic) carry the highest risk of cerebral oedema but the best spontaneous survival; subacute presentations (idiosyncratic drug injury) have less oedema but worse transplant-free survival.

In India, acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis E, A, B) and drug-induced injury (antituberculosis drugs, herbal and complementary medicines) are leading causes. Hepatitis E in pregnancy has high mortality.
Grade encephalopathy with West Haven criteria; ALF encephalopathy can progress within hours.

sections.title: First hours
items: Discuss with a liver transplant centre as soon as ALF (or severe acute liver injury with rising INR) is identified; transfer early, because patients deteriorate quickly.

Suspected paracetamol toxicity: start IV N-acetylcysteine immediately, whatever the time since ingestion and without waiting for levels. Single-dose activated charcoal if ingestion was within 4 hours and the airway is safe.
Non-paracetamol ALF: give IV N-acetylcysteine, most beneficial in early encephalopathy (grade 1 to 2) (ACG 2023; Lee 2009 trial).
Stop every potentially hepatotoxic drug, including antituberculosis drugs and herbal or dietary supplements.
Check glucose and mental state every 1 to 2 hours; treat hypoglycaemia with continuous 10% dextrose, aiming for 150 to 180 mg/dL (8.3 to 10 mmol/L). Avoid hypotonic fluids.
Admit to ICU at grade 2 encephalopathy; intubate for airway protection at grade 3 to 4.

sections.title: Cause and severity
items: INR, bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP, albumin, glucose, sodium, potassium, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine, CBC, arterial blood gas with lactate, arterial ammonia, amylase or lipase.
Paracetamol level (may be undetectable in staggered or late overdose), toxicology screen, pregnancy test in women.
Viral: IgM anti-HAV, HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc (with HBV DNA), IgM anti-HEV, HSV PCR; add HDV in HBV-positive patients.
Autoimmune markers and IgG; ceruloplasmin and urine copper for Wilson disease (very high bilirubin with very low ALP, bilirubin/ALP ratio above 2, Coombs-negative haemolysis).
Doppler ultrasound for Budd-Chiari syndrome and hepatic blood flow; blood and urine cultures and chest X-ray (infection is often clinically silent).

sections.title: Cause-specific treatment
items: Paracetamol: continue NAC beyond the standard regimen until INR is below 1.5 and clinically improving (alternative end points: ALT below 50% of peak, INR below 2, undetectable paracetamol).
HBV reactivation or flare: start entecavir or tenofovir. HSV or varicella suspected: empirical IV aciclovir until PCR results.
Acute severe autoimmune hepatitis: IV corticosteroids may be tried with transplant-centre input, but do not delay transplant assessment.
Wilson disease presenting with ALF: list for transplant early; chelation is ineffective in this setting.
HELLP syndrome or acute fatty liver of pregnancy: urgent delivery with obstetric team.
Amanita (mushroom) poisoning: contact the poisons centre; activated charcoal, NAC and silibinin (or penicillin G) per specialist advice.

sections.title: Brain, circulation, kidneys and infection
items: Arterial ammonia above 200 micromol/L predicts intracranial hypertension; below 75 micromol/L it is rare (AASLD). Start early CRRT for hyperammonaemia in grade 2 or higher encephalopathy even without a conventional renal indication (ACG 2023).
Keep serum sodium 145 to 150 mmol/L with 3% saline (250 to 500 mL bolus or infusion; keep sodium below 160 mmol/L); correct hyponatraemia by no more than 6 to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: mannitol or hypertonic saline bolus, brief hyperventilation, sedation, normothermia; ICP monitoring only in expert centres.
Lactulose and rifaximin have no proven benefit in ALF; stop lactulose in grade 3 to 4 (bowel distension hinders transplant surgery).
Hypotension: IV fluid, then noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor, adding vasopressin if needed; aim for cerebral perfusion pressure 60 to 80 mmHg.
Renal replacement: CRRT rather than intermittent haemodialysis.
INR does not predict bleeding: do not give FFP, platelets or cryoprecipitate routinely; correct only for active bleeding or high-risk procedures.

No routine prophylactic antimicrobials; do regular surveillance cultures and start empirical antibiotics (with or without antifungals) for SIRS, worsening encephalopathy, hypotension or other clinical deterioration.

sections.title: Prognosis and transplant (King's College criteria)
items: Paracetamol ALF, transplant indicated if: arterial pH below 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation; OR all three of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL (300 micromol/L) and grade 3 to 4 encephalopathy. Arterial lactate above 3 mmol/L after fluid resuscitation adds prognostic weight.

Non-paracetamol ALF: INR above 6.5 with any grade of encephalopathy; OR any three of age below 10 or above 40 years, indeterminate or drug-induced cause, jaundice to encephalopathy interval above 7 days, INR above 3.5, bilirubin above 17.5 mg/dL (300 micromol/L).
King's College criteria are specific but miss about a third of deaths; MELD predicts better in non-paracetamol ALF. Use them to trigger referral, not to delay it.
Causes with low spontaneous survival (Wilson disease, hepatitis B, idiosyncratic drug injury, autoimmune, indeterminate) need early listing discussion.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Neurological observations (GCS, pupils) and glucose every 1 to 2 hours in encephalopathy.
Magnesium and phosphate every 8 to 12 hours; INR, lactate, blood gas, creatinine, sodium and ammonia at least daily, more often in grade 2 or higher encephalopathy.
Nutrition: enteral feeding if oral intake is not expected within 5 to 7 days; protein 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg/day, starting at the lower end when ammonia exceeds 150 micromol/L.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Correcting INR with FFP: it masks the key prognostic marker and adds volume.
Late discussion with a transplant centre, or transferring a grade 3 patient without a secured airway.
Withholding NAC because the paracetamol level is low or the ingestion was late or staggered.
Missing Wilson disease, HSV hepatitis or a pregnancy-related cause; giving hypotonic fluids or sedatives before the airway is secured.

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine, paracetamol toxicity (21-hour IV regimen)
drugs.dose: 150 mg/kg IV over 15 to 60 minutes, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours
drugs.notes: In ALF continue at 100 mg/kg per 16 hours (6.25 mg/kg/h) until INR below 1.5 and improving. Cap dosing weight at 100 kg (product labelling).

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine, non-paracetamol ALF (72-hour regimen)
drugs.dose: 150 mg/kg/h IV for 1 hour, then 12.5 mg/kg/h for 4 hours, then 6.25 mg/kg/h for 67 hours
drugs.notes: Regimen from the US ALF Study Group trial (Lee 2009); benefit in encephalopathy grade 1 to 2.

drugs.name: Activated charcoal
drugs.notes: Paracetamol ingestion within 4 hours, with a protected or safe airway.

drugs.name: Dextrose 10%
drugs.dose: Continuous IV infusion titrated to blood glucose 150 to 180 mg/dL (8.3 to 10 mmol/L)
drugs.notes: Hypoglycaemia is common and worsens encephalopathy.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3%
drugs.dose: 250 to 500 mL IV bolus or continuous infusion to serum sodium 145 to 150 mmol/L (keep below 160 mmol/L)
drugs.notes: Prevention and treatment of cerebral oedema; central access preferred for infusion.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.notes: Surges of intracranial pressure; avoid in anuria unless on CRRT; check serum osmolality.

drugs.name: Aciclovir
drugs.notes: Empirical for suspected HSV or VZV hepatitis until PCR results; adjust for renal function.

drugs.name: Tenofovir disoproxil or entecavir
drugs.dose: Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg orally once daily, or entecavir 0.5 mg orally once daily
drugs.notes: HBV reactivation or severe acute HBV; adjust for renal function.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.dose: IV infusion titrated to MAP (cerebral perfusion pressure 60 to 80 mmHg)
drugs.notes: First-line vasopressor; add vasopressin if refractory.
